blocks.md: How do people guess next year's inflation? One simple answer is that they assume it will be like last year's. If prices rose 4 percent last year, they expect about 4 percent this year, and they set wages and prices accordingly. That rule looks backward and corrects itself only slowly. An alternative is that people understand how the economy works: if they know the central bank will raise rates hard after an inflation spike, they expect inflation to fall back quickly. That forward-looking view is called rational expectations.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: How expectations are formed decides whether an inflation shock dies out at once or lingers, and so how costly it is to bring inflation down.
The simplest adaptive rule sets expected inflation equal to last period's actual inflation:
More elaborate versions weight several past periods. Under **rational expectations**, $\pi^e_t$ is the model's own forecast given everything known, including policy responses.

In a three-equation model where $\pi_t = \tfrac{2}{3}\pi^e_t + \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot 2$ without shocks, a one-period supply shock that lifts inflation to 4 is followed, with $\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}$, by 3.33, 2.89, 2.59, … back toward 2. See [IS-MP-PC Model](note:is-mp-pc-model).

- Thinking adaptive expectations are never right: in a stable environment, last year's inflation is a decent forecast.
- Confusing "expectations equal last period" with "this period equals next period".
Adaptive expectations were central to Friedman's and Phelps's work on the Phillips curve in the 1960s; Robert Lucas and others developed rational expectations.
- Macro: closing the [Phillips Curve](note:phillips-curve) in the [IS-MP-PC Model](note:is-mp-pc-model); inflation persistence.
